title: After Nagasaki: Against the Politics of Psychic Numbing
author: Henry Giroux
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Nagasaki_-
_person_burned-680x529.jpg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/after-
nagasaki-against-the-politics-of-psychic-numbing/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Nagasaki_-
_person_burned-680x529.jpg)

A child burned to death in the bombing of Nagasaki. This photo, and others
like it, were banned from publication by the US military until 1952. Photo:
Yōsuke Yamahata. Public domain.

> Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed
> until it is faced.
>
> – James Baldwin
>
> You cannot understand the twentieth century without Hiroshima.
>
> – Robert J. Lifton and Greg Mitchell

Every day we scroll past photographs of burned children, bombed-out
neighborhoods, families clawing through rubble with their bare hands, and
parents carrying the bodies of sons and daughters killed beneath collapsing
concrete. Such images seldom unsettle our conscience, provoke outrage, and
awaken a demand for justice. Increasingly, they do none of these things. They
register briefly before dissolving into another statistic, another headline,
another passing image in the endless digital stream. Violence has become
familiar, suffering routine, and genocide itself is in danger of becoming just
another image consumed and forgotten..

This is not merely a political development; it is one of the great moral and
cultural disasters of our age. We have not simply become accustomed to living
amid unprecedented violence, we have been educated to accommodate it. Cruelty
no longer confronts us as an ethical rupture demanding judgment and action. It
has been absorbed into the rhythms of everyday life, stripped of its capacity
to shock, and transformed into yet another spectacle competing for our
distracted attention. As [Susan
Sontag](https://www.nybooks.com/articles/1975/02/06/fascinating-fascism/)
suggested in her analysis of fascist aesthetics, violence increasingly becomes
aestheticized—organized as spectacle, invested with the pleasures of
domination, and detached from the suffering of its victims.

Under such conditions, the dehumanization of others is inseparable from the
transformation of the machinery of death into a spectacle consumed with
fascination rather than horror. The deepest victory of authoritarian politics
in the twenty-first century lies not only in its capacity to produce immense
suffering, pain, and death, but in its ability to cultivate moral indifference
while making violence appear seductive, entertaining, or inevitable. When
people cease to feel the pain of others, violence no longer requires
widespread consent; it needs only widespread indifference.

As the anniversaries of Hiroshima and Nagasaki return once again, they do so
largely eclipsed by the Trump administration's transformation of the nation's
[two hundred and fiftieth anniversary into a spectacle of militarized
patriotism, historical mythmaking, and American
triumphalism](https://www.theatlantic.com/politics/2026/06/trump-250-great-
american-state-fair/687456/). The pageantry celebrates a narrative of national
innocence while eclipsing one of the twentieth century's greatest atrocities
committed in its name. The more urgent question, therefore, is not simply what
happened in August 1945. It is what has become of a society whose formative
institutions increasingly educate people to accommodate violence rather than
resist it.

The answer lies in more than what [Gore
Vidal](https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2014/06/02/vida-j02.html) once
described as America's cultivated historical amnesia. Under gangster
capitalism, forgetting has become a governing principle of power. We inhabit a
regime of [organized
forgetting](https://searchworks.stanford.edu/view/10643489)that erases bodies
from public consciousness even as it erases historical memory itself. It
teaches us to look without seeing, to witness without feeling, and to consume
the suffering of others as another spectacle in an endless cycle of
distraction, entertainment, and forgetting. Such regimes are not abstractions.
They become visible whenever policies capable of producing immense human
suffering disappear beneath the noise of political spectacle—as in the Trump
administration's dismantling of the United States Agency for International
Development, a policy that recent analyses estimate has already contributed to
“[an estimated 700,000 deaths
worldwide](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/29/opinion/elon-musk-far-right-
remigration.html).”

How else are we to understand a world in which more than [sixty-four thousand
Palestinian children have been killed or injured in Gaza since October
2023](https://www.unicefusa.org/stories/more-50000-children-killed-or-injured-
gaza) while their suffering disappears almost as quickly as the headlines that
briefly acknowledge it? How else do we explain the reported deaths of more
than [one hundred children in the bombing of a girls' school in
Iran](https://www.amnestyusa.org/blog/u-s-responsible-for-killing-
over-100-children-in-iran-school-attack/), an event that barely registered
before it was displaced by the next manufactured spectacle? These are not
isolated tragedies. They reveal a broader cultural condition in which atrocity
is consumed, circulated, and forgotten with astonishing speed.

This is the deepest wound inflicted by authoritarian culture. It does not
merely normalize violence; it reorganizes consciousness. It severs suffering
from compassion, history from responsibility, and death from mourning. When
the victims disappear from memory almost as quickly as they disappear from
life, power secures one of its greatest triumphs: it destroys not only bodies
but the public capacity to recognize their loss. In that moment, forgetting
becomes the final act of violence, completing in consciousness what bombs,
prisons, armies, and occupations begin in history. This cultural condition has
been analyzed most powerfully by Robert Jay Lifton.

[Robert Jay Lifton gave this condition a name: _psychic
numbing_](https://www.bostonreview.net/articles/psychic-numbing/). He used the
phrase to describe the diminished capacity to feel in the face of overwhelming
violence. What begins as a psychological defense against unbearable suffering
can become a cultural and political condition. Entire societies learn to look
without seeing, to witness without feeling, and eventually to forget. This
condition is not merely an individual affliction, or type of “[impaired
mourning](https://www.bostonreview.net/articles/psychic-numbing/)”; it is a
form of public pedagogy. It is cultivated by schools disparagment of critical
thought, historical consciousness, and civic purpose; [it is produced by media
cultures](https://www.versobooks.com/en-ca/products/214-scorched-earth)
organized around spectacle, digital platforms that reward distraction, a
culture of immediacy, and political narratives that teach us to accommodate
cruelty rather than confront it. Against this pedagogy of forgetting stands
the difficult and necessarily troubling work of historical memory.

These questions matter because remembrance is not the same as historical
memory. Official rituals of remembrance often console us by confining
catastrophe safely to the past. [As Eddie S. Glaude Jr. notes in _America,
U.S.A_](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/673832/america-usa-by-eddie-
s-glaude-jr/)., historical memory performs a very different task. It returns
us to unfinished histories whose consequences continue to inhabit the present.
[It unsettles rather than
reassures.](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/06/20/opinion/the-violence-of-
forgetting.html) It refuses the comfort of distance and insists that the past
is never truly past when the conditions that produced it survive in altered
forms. Historical memory does not ask us simply to remember what happened. It
demands that we recognize how the logics that made catastrophe possible
continue to shape the present.

Hiroshima and Nagasaki belong to precisely this kind of historical memory
because they remind us that atrocities begin long before the first bomb falls.
They begin when language is removed from moral responsibility, when history is
erased or rewritten through the vocabulary of conquest and colonization, and
when entire populations are rendered disposable before they are destroyed.
Every genocide is first a crisis of language, memory, and moral imagination.
By the time the machinery of death is set in motion, the deeper work has
already been done: compassion has been weakened, historical consciousness has
been dismantled, and violence has been normalized as common sense. Hiroshima
and Nagasaki stand not only as symbols of unprecedented destruction but also
as warnings about the political culture that makes such destruction
imaginable. Few have expressed this truth more forcefully than [the late
Howard Zinn](https://www.howardzinn.org/collection/the-bombs-of-august/):

> What means could be more horrible than the burning, mutilation, blinding,
> irradiation of hundreds of thousands of Japanese men, women, children? And
> yet it is absolutely essential for our political leaders to defend the
> bombing because if Americans can be induced to accept that, then they can
> accept any war, any means, so long as the warmakers can supply a reason. And
> there are always plausible reasons delivered from on high as from Moses on
> the Mount.

[The atomic bombings were not merely military events that concluded the Second
World War.](https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250070050/hiroshimanagasaki/)
They inaugurated a new historical formation in which scientific achievement
became inseparable from industrialized killing, technological rationality
overwhelmed ethical judgment, and civilian annihilation could be justified
through the sanitized language of military necessity, national security, and
historical inevitability. Long before the bombs incinerated cities, another
devastation had already taken place. Human beings had been transformed into
abstractions, dehumanized through racist slurs, strategic calculations, and
collateral damage.

The bomb exploded first in consciousness. [As Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o reminds
us](https://www.rile.space/books/decolonising-the-mind-the-politics-of-
language-in-african-literature), “Language as culture is the collective memory
bank of a people's experience in history.” When language is colonized, memory
itself becomes vulnerable to conquest—capturing consciousness long before it
captures territory. Long before Hiroshima and Nagasaki were reduced to ash,
language had already been emptied of moral responsibility, memory had been
rewritten in the service of empire, and entire populations had been rendered
disposable.

That moral rupture did not disappear with the mushroom clouds rising over
Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It became embedded in institutions, policies, cultural
narratives, and educational practices that normalized militarism while
celebrating technological mastery divorced from ethical restraint. The bomb
was transformed into a symbol of national virtue rather than a warning about
the abyss into which modern civilization had descended. [As Robert Jay Lifton
and Greg Mitchell observed](https://www.abebooks.com/first-edition/Hiroshima-
America-Lifton-R-Putnam-Adult/32390782043/bd), American political culture
constructed an official narrative that sought not to confront the moral
catastrophe of Hiroshima but to redeem it, converting an act of unprecedented
destruction into a story of national innocence and salvation. That narrative
did more than justify the bomb. It reorganized moral consciousness.

Lifton argued that Hiroshima did not wound only its victims; it also left a
profound mark on the American imagination, fostering a culture of denial,
moral justification, and emotional numbing. Yet he never regarded Hiroshima
solely as a source of despair. He insisted that confronting its moral legacy
honestly could foster resilience, renewal, and what [he called "survivor
wisdom](https://www.psychologytoday.com/ca/blog/psychology-and-
history/202301/retooling-for-coping-with-the-assault-on-democracy)," restoring
the historical memory and moral imagination necessary to resist future
catastrophes. That insight is even more urgent today because the habits of
denial and indifference he identified have escaped the nuclear age and become
defining features of contemporary political culture.

Among survivors of Hiroshima, this diminished capacity to feel initially
functioned as a tragic form of psychological survival. Faced with scenes too
horrific to absorb, many found themselves emotionally paralyzed, temporarily
incapable of responding to the landscape of death surrounding them. But Lifton
extended the concept much further. He argued that the same condition also
characterized those who designed the bomb, authorized its use, justified its
necessity, and later defended its moral legitimacy. What began as an emergency
psychological defense gradually became a cultural condition.

This insight reaches far beyond Hiroshima. What begins as a defense against
unbearable suffering can evolve into a political culture organized around
indifference. A society that learns not to feel one atrocity gradually
acquires the capacity to ignore others. Lifton warned that once Americans
constructed what he called a "cordon sanitaire" around Hiroshima—a barrier
protecting them from confronting its moral implications—that habit of
avoidance spread to other forms of collective suffering. The numbing did not
stop with Hiroshima. It became a way of inhabiting the world.

Nothing could better describe our present historical moment. We inhabit
societies saturated with images of catastrophe. Yet rather than enlarging our
ethical imagination, this relentless exposure often produces exhaustion,
indifference, and resignation.

Even more troubling, it feeds a resurgent war culture that glorifies
domination, celebrates militarized masculinity, and equates physical strength
with moral worth. As Susan Sontag argued in her classic essay on fascist
aesthetics, authoritarian culture does more than justify violence; it
aestheticizes it. Domination becomes seductive, hierarchy beautiful,
submission desirable, and the spectacle of power detached from the suffering
it produces. Violence no longer appears as a moral catastrophe but as an
exhilarating display of strength, discipline, virility, and national renewal.
[U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's celebration of militarized
masculinity](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/03/20/trumps-crusade-christian-
nationalism-and-the-making-of-a-holy-war/) is not simply a political posture;
it is the contemporary expression of this fascist aesthetic. It transforms
domination into virtue, physical force into moral authority, misogyny into
masculine authenticity, and violence into the highest expression of
citizenship. In doing so, it redefines citizenship itself, replacing
democratic responsibility with militarized obedience, civic courage with
warrior masculinity, and public life with a theater of force.

In such a culture, violence becomes another genre of entertainment, another
spectacle in the economy of distraction. The constant circulation of suffering
no longer enlarges compassion; it erodes it, teaching people not simply to
witness violence but increasingly to admire, consume, and normalize it.

Lifton anticipated this transformation with extraordinary clarity. As this
moral desensitization spreads, he argued, people require ever greater
spectacles of violence simply to feel anything at all. Disaster becomes
normalized, and ordinary suffering loses its capacity to disturb us.

Here the legacy of Hiroshima converges with the digital culture of the twenty-
first century.

Algorithms reward outrage while discouraging reflection. Social media
platforms monetize fear, resentment, and humiliation. Corporate news reduces
war to spectacle, compressing unbearable histories into disposable images.
Artificial intelligence accelerates the circulation of propaganda, conspiracy,
and racial mythology while diminishing the time necessary for thoughtful
judgment. We increasingly encounter suffering not as fellow human beings but
as data, content, or scrolling images. Distance becomes permanent.
Responsibility evaporates.

This is not simply a technological crisis. It is a pedagogical one.

Every culture teaches people how to see, what to value, whose lives matter,
and whose deaths may be ignored. The most powerful educational institutions
today are no longer schools alone. They are digital platforms, corporate
media, entertainment industries, and algorithmic systems that organize
attention itself. These institutions do more than distribute information. They
shape consciousness, organize attention, and cultivate habits of feeling. They
manufacture forms of identification while teaching indifference toward others.

Under such conditions, fascism no longer requires spectacular rallies or
uniforms to reproduce itself. It works more quietly and, for that reason,
often more effectively. It reshapes perception, colonizes language, erodes
historical memory, and teaches people to regard entire populations as
invaders, parasites, criminals, terrorists, or demographic threats rather than
as fellow human beings. By the time the machinery of violence is set in
motion, its deepest victory has already been won: the democratic imagination
has been hollowed out, compassion has yielded to fear, and disposability has
become common sense.

Today this pedagogy of dehumanization is once again becoming normalized. Calls
for mass deportation, fantasies of ethnic purification disguised as
"remigration," attacks on immigrants, racial conspiracy theories, and
genocidal rhetoric directed at Palestinians all depend upon a prior
educational achievement: teaching people to regard certain lives as
disposable.

[That is why figures such as Elon Musk
matter](https://www.nytimes.com/video/opinion/100000011062430/its-time-to-see-
elon-musk-for-what-he-is.html). They matter not because they are uniquely evil
but because they occupy commanding positions within the cultural apparatuses
that now educate hundreds of millions of people. When racist conspiracies,
demographic panic, and authoritarian fantasies are amplified through platforms
reaching much of the globe, white supremacist propaganda is transformed into
common sense. Hatred becomes normalized precisely because it is repeated,
circulated, rewarded, and stripped of its historical genealogy.

[As Jamelle Bouie has argued](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/29/opinion/elon-
musk-far-right-remigration.html), Musk's rhetoric is no longer confined to
coded insinuations or internet provocation. It increasingly echoes themes
drawn from the contemporary white nationalist imagination: affirming slogans
such as "First the traitors, then the invaders"; declaring that "anyone who
opposes remigration is a traitor"; amplifying demographic panic over declining
white birthrates; and normalizing the language of racial replacement and
ethnic cleansing. Bouie also notes the disturbing resonance between this
rhetoric and the political imaginary of _The Turner Diaries_ , where
"traitors" who defend a multiracial democracy are marked for elimination
before the campaign against supposed "invaders" begins. This should not be
dismissed merely as inflammatory rhetoric. Language of this kind does not
simply describe the world; it prepares people to inhabit one in which
exclusion, racial purification, and political violence appear not only
legitimate but necessary.

Yet we should resist the temptation to describe figures such as Elon Musk,
Donald Trump, Benjamin Netanyahu, or Stephen Miller simply as monsters. [As
Jorge Gonzalez Arocha observes](https://www.savageminds.co/p/nuremberg-for-
itself), the language of monstrosity may satisfy our moral outrage, but it
ultimately obscures the deeper workings of power. Monsters exist outside
history. They are imagined as aberrations, exceptions to ordinary life.
Fascism is neither. It is produced within history, cultivated through
institutions, sustained by bureaucracies, legitimized by law, amplified by
media, and normalized through the everyday pedagogies of schools, digital
platforms, entertainment industries, and political culture. When we imagine
authoritarianism as the work of monsters, we mistake symptoms for causes,
overlooking the social relations, institutional arrangements, and cultural
forces that make such politics possible.

The enduring lesson of Hiroshima is not that monsters occasionally seize
power. It is that educated people, respected institutions, celebrated
scientists, compliant journalists, and ordinary citizens can become
participants in systems that separate technical intelligence from moral
responsibility. The bureaucrats who planned Hiroshima were not monsters. The
scientists who perfected the bomb were not monsters. The journalists who
celebrated it were not monsters. They were products of institutions that
transformed mass death into administrative necessity and moral obligation. The
greatest crimes of modernity are rarely committed outside civilization; they
are committed in its name.

The political danger of the language of monstrosity is that it individualizes
what is fundamentally systemic. It encourages us to search for evil
personalities rather than authoritarian cultures, for pathological leaders
rather than the pedagogical apparatuses that educate people into accepting
cruelty, disposability, and organized forgetting. Remove one authoritarian
leader and another will take his place so long as the institutions, economic
interests, media ecosystems, and educational forces that manufacture
authoritarian consciousness remain intact. That is the enduring lesson of
Hiroshima, and it remains the central political lesson of our own time.

History never repeats itself mechanically. Gaza is not Hiroshima. Nagasaki is
not Gaza. Their histories are different, their contexts distinct. But they
reveal a recurring political logic: civilian populations rendered disposable,
overwhelming violence justified as necessity, bureaucratic language replacing
ethical judgment, and technological superiority mistaken for moral legitimacy.
Whenever human beings become abstractions rather than persons, the conditions
for atrocity are already present.

This is why remembering Nagasaki matters. Historical comparison is valuable
not because it erases difference but because it reveals recurring political
logics.

Historical memory breaks the spell of moral indifference. It restores the
connection between feeling and judgment, conscience and politics. It reminds
us that every genocide begins not with the machinery of death but with the
pedagogy of dehumanization. Long before bodies are destroyed, language is
corrupted, history is erased, compassion is ridiculed, and entire populations
are taught to disappear morally before they disappear physically.

Lifton believed that confronting Hiroshima could become a source of renewal
because it enabled us to recover our moral imagination, relearn how to feel,
and reconnect ourselves to the broader human project. That may be the most
important lesson Nagasaki offers today.

The struggle against fascism begins not only by resisting authoritarian
institutions but by refusing the moral indifference upon which they depend.
Against organized forgetting and manufacture illiteracy and amnesia, we must
recover historical memory. Against the politics of disposability, we must
insist upon the irreducible dignity of every human life. Against the seductive
myths of technological omnipotence and permanent war, we must reclaim a
language capable of naming both truth and justice.

The authoritarian abyss is no longer a distant possibility. It has entered the
present. It appears wherever democracy yields to militarism, wherever cruelty
is celebrated as strength, wherever historical memory is erased, and wherever
entire peoples are stripped of their humanity in the name of security, racial
purity, or national destiny. The forces that produced Hiroshima and Nagasaki
have not disappeared; they have assumed new languages, new technologies, and
new justifications.

The question is no longer whether we remember Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The
question is whether we can recover the moral urgency necessary to prevent
their logic from becoming the defining political grammar of the twenty-first
century. Historical memory is no longer simply an act of remembrance; it has
become a condition of survival. To remember is to resist. But memory cannot
remain a sanctuary for conscience; it must become a catalyst for collective
struggle. Its highest purpose is not simply to preserve the past but to
interrupt/rupture/transform the present. Only when remembrance gives rise to
solidarity, organized resistance, and the struggle to create a more just world
does it honor those whose lives history has tried to erase.

Numbing](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/07/after-nagasaki-against-the-
politics-of-psychic-numbing/) appeared first on
[CounterPunch.org](https://www.counterpunch.org).
